activities.title: Ways People Travelled
activities.body: Transport means the ways people travel from place to place. People have always been interested in travelling. Vehicles are things used for travel, such as carts, cars, trains, boats, and ships. In earlier years, there were far fewer vehicles. Long before that, people travelled on foot or used animals. Boats were probably the first transport invented by humans.

activities.title: The TTh Column
activities.body: The place value chart now has a TTh column. TTh stands for ten thousand. Ten Ones make one Ten. Ten Tens make one Hundred. Ten Hundreds make one Thousand. Ten Thousands make Ten Thousand. A comma helps us read large numbers easily. Numbers beyond 10,000 are written like numbers below 9,999. The number 9,123 has 9 Thousands, 1 Hundred, 2 Tens, and 3 Ones.

activities.title: Ways of travelling
activities.body: Long ago, travellers used animals for journeys. Bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules and elephants helped them travel. Camels were used in deserts. Today, people use bicycles, motorbikes, cars, buses, trains, ships and aeroplanes. Submarines travel deep underwater, while spacecraft carry people into outer space. Different journeys cover very different distances each hour.

activities.context: Reema is checking how everyday objects turn. A door with a hinge swings around its hinge, while tongs, scissors, and a file cover can also be turned. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction with the tongs. She also holds one straw steady while turning another straw around it. Later, she sees that the minute hand has returned to its initial position and wonders which movements show full turns, half turns, or everyday turns.
activities.prompt: Reema turns the door with a hinge until it returns to its starting position. What kind of turn has she made?
options: A full turn that makes a complete circle
A half turn that makes a half-moon shape
A back-and-forth movement that never goes around
A straight movement away from the hinge

why.A half turn that makes a half-moon shape: This would stop halfway around and make a half-moon shape.
why.A back-and-forth movement that never goe: Going back and forth does not make a complete circle.
why.A straight movement away from the hinge: Moving straight away from the hinge is not a turn around the hinge.

activities.explanation: Correct: returning to the starting position after going around shows a complete circle.

activities.context: Reema is checking how everyday objects turn. A door with a hinge swings around its hinge, while tongs, scissors, and a file cover can also be turned. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction with the tongs. She also holds one straw steady while turning another straw around it. Later, she sees that the minute hand has returned to its initial position and wonders which movements show full turns, half turns, or everyday turns.
activities.prompt: What happens when Reema takes two half turns in the same direction with the tongs?
options: The turns make a full turn, and the tongs return to the starting position
The turns make only a half turn, and the tongs stop halfway around
The turns remain separate, and the tongs do not return to the start
The tongs stay at the halfway point because the turns do not join

why.The turns make only a half turn, and the: One half turn would stop at the halfway point, not two.
why.The turns remain separate, and the tongs: Half turns in the same direction continue around and complete the circle.
why.The tongs stay at the halfway point beca: The turns do join, so the tongs do not remain at the halfway point.

activities.explanation: Correct: two half turns in the same direction complete one full turn.

activities.context: Reema is checking how everyday objects turn. A door with a hinge swings around its hinge, while tongs, scissors, and a file cover can also be turned. Reema takes two half turns in the same direction with the tongs. She also holds one straw steady while turning another straw around it. Later, she sees that the minute hand has returned to its initial position and wonders which movements show full turns, half turns, or everyday turns.
activities.prompt: Reema sees that the minute hand has returned to its initial position. Why has this happened?
options: The minute hand has made a full turn and completed a complete circle
The minute hand has made only a half turn and stopped halfway
The minute hand has stayed still at the initial position
The minute hand has moved back and forth without going around

why.The minute hand has made only a half tur: A half turn would leave the hand halfway around.
why.The minute hand has stayed still at the: Staying still does not show a completed turn.
why.The minute hand has moved back and forth: Moving back and forth does not make a complete circle.

activities.explanation: Correct: the minute hand returns to its initial position after a full turn.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a full turn and a half turn?
activities.answer: A full turn makes a complete circle and returns a turning object to its initial position. A half turn can make a half-moon shape, so it covers only part of the circle. The minute hand returns to its initial position after a full turn, showing the result of completing the whole circle.
points: Full turn makes a complete circle
Full turn returns the object to its initial position
Half turn can make a half-moon shape
Half turn covers only part of the circle
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Learners are making a paper fan from a rectangular sheet of paper, folding it every 2 cm. They open the fan while keeping one side fixed so that the turns can be seen. They also build a house with notebook covers and mark its angles. One part of the house has a five-sided shape containing two right angles, two obtuse angles and one acute angle.
activities.prompt: A learner forgets the required spacing when making the rectangular paper fan. What should the learner do next?
options: Make the folds again, 2 cm apart.
Make the folds again, with uneven spacing.
Make the folds again, but only along one edge.
Make the folds again, using a different measurement.

why.Make the folds again, with uneven spacin: Uneven spacing does not follow the stated folding rule.
why.Make the folds again, but only along one: Folding only one edge misses the stated fan-making method.
why.Make the folds again, using a different: A different measurement does not match the required 2 cm spacing.

activities.explanation: This restores the required spacing of every 2 cm.

activities.context: Learners are making a paper fan from a rectangular sheet of paper, folding it every 2 cm. They open the fan while keeping one side fixed so that the turns can be seen. They also build a house with notebook covers and mark its angles. One part of the house has a five-sided shape containing two right angles, two obtuse angles and one acute angle.
activities.prompt: In the house's five-sided shape, one of the two right angles is changed into an acute angle. What set of angles would then be marked?
options: One right angle, two obtuse angles and two acute angles.
Two right angles, one obtuse angle and two acute angles.
Two right angles, two obtuse angles and no acute angles.
One right angle, one obtuse angle and three acute angles.

why.Two right angles, one obtuse angle and t: An obtuse angle was not changed, so two should remain.
why.Two right angles, two obtuse angles and: The changed angle becomes acute instead of being removed.
why.One right angle, one obtuse angle and th: Only one right angle changes, so the two obtuse angles remain.

activities.explanation: One right angle changes, leaving one right, two obtuse and two acute angles.

activities.prompt: Explain how the learners should fold and open the paper fan, and how they should classify its turns.
activities.answer: Fold the paper every 2 cm to make the fan. Keep one side fixed so its turns can be seen. A turn smaller than a quarter turn is acute, a quarter turn is right, and a turn larger than a quarter but smaller than a half is obtuse.
points: Fold the rectangular paper every 2 cm.
Keep one side fixed while showing the turns.
Classify a turn smaller than a quarter as acute.
Classify quarter and larger-than-quarter turns correctly.

activities.answer: The learner folds a circle into 8 equal parts, attaches a straw at the centre, and marks a starting point. The straw can then be used to show an eighth turn. These steps make the angle measuring tool from the equal parts of the circle and its centre straw.
points: Folds the circle into 8 equal parts
Attaches a straw at the centre
Marks a starting point
Uses the straw to show an eighth turn

activities.context: During an activity, children look at angles in shapes and make initial guesses about them. They then check the guesses with an angle-measuring tool, and sometimes they need a combination of measures. The measured angles are described as acute, right or obtuse. The children use a combination of measuring tools to verify those turns, then draw angles for the given turn measures using given lines.
activities.prompt: What should the children do after making an initial guess about an angle in a shape?
options: Test the estimate with an angle-measuring tool.
Keep the estimate without checking it.
Check the estimate by describing the angle only.
Replace the angle in the shape with a drawn angle.

A guess alone does not confirm the measure.
why.Check the estimate by describing the ang: A description does not replace measuring the angle.
why.Replace the angle in the shape with a dr: Drawing a new angle does not check the original angle.

activities.explanation: The tool is used to check the guess.

activities.prompt: After verifying the arrow turns, what should the children do with the given turn measures and lines?

Guess the angles and leave the given lines unused.
Measure another angle instead of following the turn measures.
Check the turns but do not draw the requested angles.

why.Guess the angles and leave the given lin: Leaving the lines unused does not complete the drawing task.
why.Measure another angle instead of followi: Another angle would not represent the given turn measures.
why.Check the turns but do not draw the requ: Stopping after checking would leave the drawing task unfinished.

activities.explanation: The final task asks for angles to be drawn using the given lines.

activities.prompt: Explain why children should check a guessed angle measure with an angle-measuring tool.
activities.answer: The guess gives children an idea of what to expect, but the angle-measuring tool checks the angle. If the guess is different, they can correct it. The checked angle can then be described as acute, right or obtuse.
points: A guess is an initial idea
The tool checks the angle
A wrong guess can be corrected
The checked angle can be classified

activities.context: During a classroom activity, the teacher showed pictures of creatures that had each made a quarter turn once. She reminded the children that clock-hand movement is clockwise movement, while the opposite movement is anti-clockwise movement. The children could observe each direction by opening a tap, unscrewing a lid, or loosening a nut. The teacher then gave directions to rotate, and the children completed a table showing the directions they would face.
activities.prompt: In the table case that starts at North and gives two right angles clockwise, what direction will the children face at the end?

East is reached after only the first right angle.
West would require an anti-clockwise turn from North.
North is the starting direction, not the final direction.

activities.explanation: Two clockwise right angles from North end at South.

Two anti-clockwise right angles from South reach North.
East is the direction after the first turn.
West is not reached by two anti-clockwise right angles from South.

activities.explanation: From South, the first anti-clockwise right angle reaches East.

activities.prompt: Explain how to complete the table case that starts at North and gives two right angles clockwise.

The first clockwise right angle reaches East.
The second clockwise right angle reaches South.
